query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Consolidating the nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 via a rapid sintering method (e.g., spark plasma sintering at an optimized intermediate temperature) will coarsen the grain structure to a stable ultrafine scale that minimizes radiation‐induced Cr/V segregation precipitation while preserving the defect sink effectiveness that underlies the observed negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibiting a high density of grain boundaries that, under irradiation, foster the formation of Cr/V-rich precipitates.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step consolidation via spark plasma sintering (SPS) at an intermediate temperature that is high enough to coarsen the grains to an ultrafine scale yet low enough to avoid triggering unwanted thermal precipitation during processing.
generation.conditions: Energetic-particle irradiation under fusion relevant conditions up to approximately 8 dpa, with operational temperatures maintained below the onset of thermal instability (likely below ~800–1000 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and internal interfaces rearranged during consolidation that offer defect sinks; the slightly coarser, homogenized ultrafine microstructure reduces local chemical potential gradients responsible for phase separation.
generation.mechanism: The controlled grain coarsening reduces the driving force for radiation-induced segregation of Cr/V by lowering localized concentration gradients while maintaining enough interfaces to annihilate irradiation-induced defects, thus preventing the formation of undesired second-phase precipitates without causing additional irradiation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified fully nanocrystalline alloy, the consolidated ultrafine-grained bulk material will show a significant reduction or suppression in the formation of Cr/V-rich precipitates under irradiation (at ~8 dpa) while retaining near-negligible irradiation hardening, and will additionally be more amenable to practical bulk fabrication.
generation.baseline: The original nanocrystalline alloy exhibits radiation-induced Cr/V precipitation (as observed in earlier studies) with negligible irradiation hardening, yet its nanostructured state poses challenges for bulk processing and long-term thermal stability.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under irradiation up to 8 dpa, at temperatures low enough to prevent further thermal coarsening (likely below ~800–1000 K), and for fusion-relevant particle fluxes where defect production rates are comparable to those in reported experiments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal SPS processing parameters (temperature, time, cooling rate) required to achieve the desired ultrafine grain structure without inducing any new phases are yet to be determined, and the quantitative extent of precipitation suppression remains to be measured.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using the proposed SPS consolidation to produce an ultrafine-grained bulk version of W38Ta36Cr15V11, and a control set retaining the original nanocrystalline structure. Subject both to energetic-particle irradiation under fusion-relevant conditions up to 8 dpa. Characterize post-irradiation microstructures (using TEM and atom probe tomography) and perform nanoindentation tests to assess hardness.
measurements: Quantitative TEM/atom probe tomography for Cr/V-rich precipitate volume fraction and size distribution
Nanoindentation hardness measurements pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed sample exhibits no significant reduction in Cr/V-rich precipitates relative to the unmodified material, or if its irradiation-induced hardening is significantly higher, then the hypothesis that the consolidation step prevents radiation-induced precipitation while retaining low hardening is falsified.

## Abstract
Are high-entropy alloys the solution to radiation damage? AbstractA body-centered cubic W-based refractory high entropy alloy with outstanding radiation resistance has been developed. The alloy was grown as thin films showing a bimodal grain size distribution in the nanocrystalline and ultrafine regimes and a unique 4-nm lamella-like structure revealed by atom probe tomography (APT). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and x-ray diffraction show certain black spots appearing after thermal annealing at elevated temperatures. TEM and APT analysis correlated the black spots with second-phase particles rich in Cr and V. No sign of irradiation-created dislocation loops, even after 8 dpa, was observed. Furthermore, nanomechanical testing shows a large hardness of 14 GPa in the as-deposited samples, with near negligible irradiation hardening. Theoretical modeling combining ab initio and Monte Carlo techniques predicts the formation of Cr- and V-rich second-phase particles and points at equal mobilities of point defects as the origin of the exceptional radiation tolerance.
